archetype.name: Point Guard (play-action distributor)
archetype.definition: A rhythm-and-timing passer who wins by putting Shanahan's under-center play-action concepts on schedule, spreading the ball to Kittle, McCaffrey and whoever is winning outside, and extending plays with his legs only when the structure breaks.

report.headline: Top-five efficiency built early; with receivers vanishing, the second half gets harder.
report.take:
Purdy is having one of the league's best passing seasons on a per-play basis: 0.289 EPA per dropback (5th of 49), 8.39 yards per attempt (6th), a 7.2% TD rate (5th) and the league's 3rd-lowest sack rate, all for the NFL's top-ranked offense by EPA. That's in line with who he has been. His career has two seasons ranked 1st and 6th in EPA per play, and his completion percentage over expected has sat around the top five three times. The system helps, and he runs it at a high level. Under center his CPOE is 14.5 against 0.8 from shotgun, which tells you how much of his accuracy comes from play-action timing and defined reads.

The headline numbers, though, lean on two September games against bad defenses. He posted 23.3 and 22.9 EPA against Miami (32nd in defense now) and Arizona (29th), and nothing since has come close. Over his last five games his EPA per dropback is 0.12, 0.168 below his season mark; over the last three his TD rate is 4.3% and his INT rate 3.2%. That's still above the league average of -0.002, but it's good-starter efficiency, not MVP efficiency. The yardage hasn't moved. He's averaging 261.3 a game over the last three. What dried up is the touchdowns and the explosive margin, and the interceptions crept in.

The biggest single driver of his efficiency has been Mike Evans: 40 targets at 1.023 EPA each, for 40.9 EPA, far more than Kittle's 14.9 on more targets. Downfield and over the middle is where the value lives: 0.545 EPA on throws of 10+ air yards, 0.68 to the middle, 1.148 on 20 deep shots with no picks. Evans is out this week, Deebo Samuel is out, Christian Kirk is on IR, and Brandon Aiyuk is only just back from the reserve/left squad list on a two-week roster exemption. The Purdy who goes to Dallas is throwing to Kittle, McCaffrey, Jordan Watkins and depth pieces.

The parts that should hold are the pocket management and the red-zone efficiency. He has turned his pressure-to-sack rate from a weakness early in his career into a strength for two straight years. The parts that should cool are the 12-touchdown, zero-interception red-zone line and a TD pace (36 over 17 games) that came mostly in September. Expect a quarterback who stays clearly above average in a top offense. What decides whether he's top-five or merely top-twelve the rest of the way is how quickly Evans and Aiyuk get back on the field.

strengths.title: Pressure no longer becomes sacks
strengths.body: His 3.3% sack rate ranks 3rd and only 17.9% of his pressures turn into sacks, 5th best. That's a genuine change from earlier in his career, when he sat 37th and 26th in pressure-to-sack. Last year he ranked 5th too, so two years in a row says this is now a skill rather than luck. Part of it is the offensive line: the 49ers allow the 3rd-lowest hit rate in the league. He has also learned to escape: 19 scrambles average 1.019 EPA and produced 12 first downs.

strengths.title: Damage beyond 10 yards and over the middle
strengths.body: Throws of 10+ air yards return 0.545 EPA per attempt against 0.178 underneath, and the middle of the field runs at 0.68 EPA with a 9.0 CPOE. That's the Shanahan play-action menu working: crossers and seams off run action, thrown on time. The concept is sustainable. The magnitude, especially the 1.148 EPA on just 20 deep throws, leaned heavily on Evans and will shrink without him.

strengths.title: Under-center accuracy and red-zone finishing
strengths.body: From under center his CPOE is 14.5 and his success rate 0.597, both well above his shotgun marks. That's where the scheme makes his reads easiest. In the red zone he's thrown 12 touchdowns and no interceptions on 41 attempts at 0.631 EPA. The skill is real, but a perfect red-zone ledger on that volume will give some back.

concerns.title: Efficiency has been sliding since September
concerns.body: Since Week 4 his EPA per dropback is 0.12, down 0.168 from his season figure. His two monster games came against Miami and Arizona, now 32nd and 29th in defense. Against Seattle (5th) he was negative, and he managed only modest EPA against Washington and Atlanta. Some of this is schedule and some is touchdown regression. Either way, the season line overstates the quarterback of the last month.

concerns.title: Receiving corps gutted right now
concerns.body: Evans' 40.9 EPA is the largest single slice of his passing value, and Evans is out, along with Samuel, Kirk (IR) and Aiyuk (roster exemption). This is the most important variable on his outlook because it's about personnel, not form. Jordan Watkins' 0.952 EPA per target is promising but comes on only 13 targets. Kittle and McCaffrey are dependable but far less explosive.

concerns.title: Interceptions are who he is
concerns.body: His 2.1% INT rate ranks 28th of 49. The 3.2% over the last three games is worse, and three of his five picks came on intermediate throws. That isn't new: he ranked 55th, 50th and 49th in interceptions over the past three seasons. It's the cost of an aggressive middle-of-the-field approach, so treat the September stretch of few picks as the outlier, not the norm.

trend.note: Two 20-plus EPA games in Weeks 2 and 3 were followed by a run between -2 and 8.5 EPA a game. Week 9 against the Raiders (28th in defense) was a mild bounce, but against a soft opponent.

nextGame.headline: Soft Dallas secondary, but who catches the ball?
nextGame.body:
Dallas is about as friendly a pass defense as he'll see: 31st in defensive EPA and 29th against the pass. It's 26th on short throws, which is the area his depleted receiver group will have to work in, and its pass rush is middling (23rd in sack rate). The Book's 55.5 total and SF -3.5 line expect points. Dallas' offense ranks 6th, which should keep him throwing into the second half. The one cautionary signal is that offenses run on Dallas more than usual (pass rate over norm -4, 29th), and Dallas is 30th against the run. Shanahan could lean on McCaffrey and the ground game rather than ask a patchwork receiver room to win outside.

Availability cuts both ways. On his side, Evans, Samuel and Kirk are out and Aiyuk isn't active yet, which removes most of his explosive downfield targets. On theirs, corner Joey Porter Jr. and safety P.J. Locke are out and linebacker DeMarvion Overshown is too, with Donovan Ezeiruaku questionable. That thins the coverage behind which Kittle and the crossers work. Dallas is also missing George Pickens and Jake Ferguson, which could dull its offense and the shootout script. The early forecast shows 14 mph wind with 25 mph gusts, but the stadium has a retractable roof that will likely be closed, so don't build anything on it.

keyMatchups.title: Whoever is WR1 against Dallas
keyMatchups.body: Dallas has let opponents' top receivers outscore their own averages by more than any defense in the league, and it ranks 25th in EPA allowed to that role. With Evans and Samuel out, Purdy's outside volume likely funnels to Watkins. Watkins has been efficient on a small sample, and Porter's absence widens the window.

keyMatchups.title: Kittle over the middle
keyMatchups.body: Kittle leads the team with 53 targets, and Dallas sits 23rd in EPA allowed to tight ends. Purdy's middle-of-the-field throws are his most efficient area. With Overshown out and Locke concussed, the seams and crossers should be there.

keyMatchups.title: Run-heavy script could cap volume
keyMatchups.body: Dallas is 30th against the run, and opponents run on it more than normal. It is, however, 2nd-stingiest in EPA to lead backs, so McCaffrey's checkdowns may not add much. If the 49ers grind it on the ground with a thin receiver group, Purdy's efficiency could stay high while his yardage settles near his average.

nextGame.watch: How the 49ers distribute targets without Evans and Samuel: does Watkins handle the outside volume and get the intermediate shots, or does the offense shrink to Kittle, McCaffrey and screens?

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is solid: a top offensive line in hit rate, a scheme that makes his under-center reads easy, sack avoidance he has now shown for two seasons, and a top-ten rushing contribution from scrambles. That should keep him comfortably above league-average efficiency all year. The September ceiling of 36 touchdowns on pace and 0.289 EPA per dropback is unlikely to return. The red-zone perfection and the TD rate (7.2% against a league 4.3%) are already cooling. His interception history says the INT rate settles closer to 2.5% than to his early-season lows.

Expect something close to his last five games until the receiver room heals: about 240 yards a game, about 1.5 to 1.8 touchdowns, 0.12 to 0.22 EPA per dropback. Evans' and Aiyuk's return dates are estimates. If both are back and healthy by December, the deep and middle-of-the-field explosiveness that powered his first month should come with them, and the upper end of these ranges becomes the likelier case.
swingFactors: Timing and health of Mike Evans' return
Aiyuk's ramp-up after the roster exemption
Red-zone TD rate regressing from 12 TDs, 0 INTs

confidence.note: An eight-game sample skewed by two soft early opponents, and a receiver room in flux.
